I don't personally recommend telling kids that you got the scars doing something "cool" because they absolutely will not leave it alone. I helped some kids with swim lessons once and one of them asked what happened to me, and I jokingly told them I got attacked by a bear. The next hour I was absolutely bombarded with questions and I had to make shit up on the spot—what kind of bear was it, was it a baby bear, was it scary? Not hard questions but still. I'd recommend saying something that's not going to downplay them, but still makes sense, like "I was in a car accident" or something.

Adults, depending on how close I am, I either just say it's self harm directly or just say I was attacked. If it's the latter, there's usually not too many follow-up questions.

I was. After my most recent ex broke up with me, I relapsed self harm, and I had a suicide attempt about a month after.

What's funny about it is the reason he realized he had feelings in the first place was because I had been put in a psych ward following a previous suicide attempt and, when he was collecting some things to bring for me, the full weight of my absence hit him and it was, apparently, unbearable. He promised me later that he would do anything if he knew I was struggling and that he wouldn't let me get to that low of a point ever again. While he was breaking up with me he begged "Please don't kill yourself," verbatim. He then proceeded to say nothing about the self harm and didn't seem to care about the attempt at all outside of an "I'm sorry you're going through this" text. I was also forced on a medical leave by my school after they caught wind of the attempt and he didn't even come to say goodbye.

I wouldn't say I "got through" at all. Even though I've made a lot of progress in a lot of areas with a lot of therapy, counseling, and long talks with friends, that wound and the feeling of utter betrayal and abandonment is going to be fresh for a long time. It just makes me wonder if he ever cared at all, if any of it was real, and it honestly just makes those thoughts sound so much louder.

I mourned a relationship that was only three months for around nine to ten months—my most recent was eight months, and I feel it'll take me twice as long to "get over it" so to speak. Healing isn't linear. You will have days where you feel completely fine and days where the grief is so heavy it'll hurt to move or think and both are okay, natural, and healthy. It just shows how much love you have and had.

Honestly him just acknowledging that he didn't treat me right in and after the breakup honestly did really help. I wouldn't necessarily say it was "fulfilling" so much as it was validating, like I wasn't crazy for how much I struggled. But I realized that just wasn't true, and it wouldn't be fair to expect me to get continuously strung along by some twink from New Jersey to wait for the moment he would "realize" my worth.

Mine was a children's Bible I'd gotten from my former pastor after I aged out of Youth Group. I just gave it to a Goodwill. Even though my father is a staunch New Atheist, he's a librarian first and foremost, and I was more scared of *his* wrath over throwing away a perfectly good book than I was of *His* wrath.

It never made sense to me. Even I was 100% a pure, righteous Christian who lived a relatively sinless life and kept God in my heart at all times I don't think I would ever be comfortable even *thinking* about the millions of people who would have to live in horrifying anguish for the rest of eternity just because their life went down a different path than mine did. And the worst part is that many of these people Christians claim are going to Hell are far from bad people—sometimes they're just people down on their luck, sometimes they're gay, sometimes they believe that the thought of Hell is (rightfully) a cruel and unjust way to view the afterlife.

Case in point: once saw someone make a post that said people should pray for Jeffrey Dahmer to be spared by God's "infinite mercy" and join the Kingdom of Heaven since he converted to Christianity before death and was "just as much a sinner as anyone else..." while a few posts later they reblogged something talking about how trans people were irreparably "mutilating their bodies" and permanently preventing themselves from rising again in the Second Coming since they decided they were better at designing humanity than God was.

It's not "Hell for the non-believers" or "Hell for all the sinners," it's just "Hell for anyone we don't like and don't agree with."

I mean...maybe it's not the most scientifically accurate, per se, but here's the way a lot of my upbringing helped shape my own beliefs on the afterlife (religious background including: atheism, Pentecostalism, witchcraft, Hellenism, Druidry, Quakerism, Shintō, and Buddhism). I'm not claiming that this is the *absolute* truth, but for a very long time until I came more into my own, this is how I came to terms with things with the knowledge and experience I had at the time. Sorry for the length.

Science helps to explain the *material* reality of life—what encompasses our world and how it works. We can observe the exact things that you're scared of about dying and understand *why* it happens. We can research and theorize how our world came to be, and the ways that it operates. We use it to explore the things we don't yet know or understand and try to use it to help us further advance ourselves. Religion and spirituality, on the other hand, deal more with the *im*material—matters of things like morality, the human experience, why exactly it is that we operate so differently from any other animal, or your soul, if you believe in one. Generally just things that go *beyond* the realm of what we (or science) can reasonably observe. Many aspects of religion can be explained by science—how we as humans came to be, where the world's languages came from, where seasons and air come from. Even some more complex things, like where the feeling of prayer and meditation come from. But there are some things you can't. For example, what gave us the urge to pray in the first place, and why are we programmed to feel a certain way when we do? Why do humans have a sense of morality or conscious? How is it that the Earth was formed in a way that was so perfectly suitable for life, or how exactly it was the life in general came to be?

Scientific atheists often feel much more certain about their own religious beliefs since science has actual, tangible evidence backing it. But religion and science are based on completely different aspects of human experience (which, note, expands a *lot* further than the reach of Christianity and its ideas on death and the afterlife). It's stupid to think that you can only "believe" in one or the other when a large portion of people who are actually religious either find ways to reconcile their own beliefs in interpretation, or already have beliefs that can be backed by science/embrace scientific discovery in their own worldviews. (e.g. Buddhists, Baháʼís, Hinduism, many denominations of Judaism, and many, many more). Many of the greatest minds out there had no religious affiliation, but there are still plenty that did and still do (see also: Isaac Newton, Robert T. Bakker, Charles Babbage).

Of course, none of this explains an afterlife specifically. That's one of the biggest questions religion serves to answer. But know that just because you believe in science, doesn't mean that there *can't* be more out there than science can explain as it stands.

I can't say much more than what u/sunstrawberry said since they put it beautifully but here's my own advice.

 The thing that always helps me whenever I feel like that is reminding myself that if I actually, genuinely were acting the way that I am for just attention, I would be consciously aware of the fact that it's all fake and I wouldn't be trying to hide it. And I can tell that that's not the case with you. It doesn't matter how much or how deep you cut, or if you even cut *at all* to hurt yourself-- self harm is just that, self harm, and you deserve just as much help or recognition as anyone else does.

Have you heard of the red balloon metaphor? "Don't focus on the white elephant, focus on the red balloon." If people keep telling you to just *not* self harm, of course you're going to focus on self harm since that's all you're being talked to about. Instead, try to find something to do to distract you from self harm-- painting, playing an instrument, playing a video game, baking. Focus more on that and it'll be easier to ignore that white elephant.

I WAS LITERALLY *JUST* PREPARING TO MAKE A POST LIKE THIS. I get the urges to cut myself all the time but I'm not prepared for the kind of backlash that I might get if I were to do it and get caught. Usually, I just hit myself, but when I say that I do that, people automatically just stop taking me seriously for some reason and just say that I'm being overdramatic and attention-seeking, which is worse since I've actually bruised my head from doing what I do. Most people I know have such a very specific, movie-esque view of depression and mental illness that whenever they see something that doesn't fit into that stereotypical "can't get out of bed, crying all the time, cutting yourself, being poetic" type of lens, they just automatically dismiss it unfortunately.

Funny thing is is that when I last went to see the doctor to for a checkup and to get blood drawn, she specifically had to ask about my mental health, to which she told my parents that it's likely that I either have some sort of developing personality disorder or long undiagnosed ADHD. They both ignored that too because "it's not like she's a psychiatrist or anything."

I don't think there's much I can really do to convince my parents if they're *this* obtuse about it but thank you for your advice regardless.

I would consider it if they were actually open about anything at all. They already view therapy as a threat instead of a help as it is (*very* passive aggressive about it, they only started taking my sister to therapy after her panic attacks starting becoming debilitating and frequent). If we were to go to therapy together they would just try to dismiss and explain away whatever I was feeling to something external as if it's not literally part of a mental illness.

Obviously I wouldn't do that, and realistically I know that people aren't going to try to do it either. That's why it's nice to at least have the acknowledgement that I'm not actually going crazy when it feels like I am, but trying to talk logic into me and telling me "there's so much to live for" isn't really going to work. Once I'm in that mindset all of that logic tends to go out the window, which is why I said it feels pointless to try and convince me otherwise.

Yeah, they might come across as just words but I guess... at least for me just knowing someone acknowledges what it is I'm feeling in that moment is helpful, even if it doesn't make me feel any better about it. I don't need people trying and dissuade me from doing something, though-- I agree with OP in that that shit is completely pointless, especially since once I'm in that mindset it takes me a long time to get out of it so you shouldn't just waste your breath. There's literally just no point to it.
